title: A causal, measurement-grade account of conscious content

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory that connects particular experiences, such as seeing a color or recognizing a face, to the physical brain processes that support them. It would make independently testable predictions about which features a person experiences, provide measurements with characterized reliability and limits, and support selective interventions that alter a specified experienced feature. Feature binding belongs within this explanatory target, including how color, shape, identity and background become a unified experience.

As a synthesis of the proposed goal, success would require agreement among prediction, measurement and intervention. A theory would need to explain why a particular neural process supports a specified conscious content, predict when that content occurs, and anticipate the effects of manipulating the process. Its measurements would need to distinguish experienced content from changes in attention, memory, recognition and the ability to communicate an experience. The proposed demonstrations establish selective suppression of a feature. Selectively creating or restoring that feature would require further evidence.

significance.text: If demonstrated, this account would connect subjective perceptual features to physical mechanisms through prospective prediction and causal intervention. It would advance the explanation of how distributed processing supports a unified experience and provide a basis for measuring particular contents within validated conditions. That combination would constitute a fundamental neuroscience advance. Its feasibility remains uncertain.

Clinical motivation comes from the difficulty of recognizing consciousness in patients with limited behavioral responses. A validated measure could improve decisions for some patients with disorders of consciousness. Applications to anesthesia monitoring and infant assessment are conditional downstream possibilities requiring separate validation in those populations and settings. A measure that predicts recovery could aid prognosis, while establishing the contents of an experience would require additional evidence.

Scope synthesis places limits on the broader implications. Explaining perceptual content would leave further work on whether reported intentions causally influence actions beyond unconscious preparation. Attributing consciousness to artificial systems implementing an apparently similar process would require additional assumptions and evidence about transfer across implementations. The question of why a physical process is experienced could also remain. Legal or institutional changes would depend on social judgments and decisions following the scientific advance.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central missing capability is an independently predictive, causal account of specified conscious contents and their binding. The 2025 adversarial study illustrates the need for precise predictions that distinguish competing accounts and expose them to possible failure. It challenged particular biological predictions of integrated information theory, or IIT, and global neuronal workspace theory, or GNWT, while supporting others. A successor account must address those mixed findings and make additional discriminating predictions.

A major scientific barrier is identifying which neural events are causally responsible for a conscious feature. Decoding stimulus information from brain activity establishes that information is available in the measured signals. Establishing its role in experience requires further evidence. Selective intervention must separate a change in experience from impaired attention, memory, recognition, reporting or motor response. Preservation of early sensory responses provides one useful dissociation, but leaves several of these explanations open.

Binding adds the challenge of explaining how distinct and distributed feature-processing mechanisms support a seamless experience. An account must predict when features are experienced together and when they dissociate. Measurement becomes especially difficult when a person cannot report an experience. Behavioral responsiveness is observable, while its relationship to subjective experience introduces uncertainty into clinical and anesthetic assessments. These difficulties affect both the construction of a measure and the reference evidence used to validate it.

Engineering synthesis identifies further requirements for a usable system. The theory would need explicit predictions at the spatial and temporal resolution available to its measurements and interventions, reliable uncertainty estimates, and clearly specified operating conditions. Clinical use would additionally require robustness to differences in brain injury, medication and response ability. The supplied evidence leaves open whether one account can satisfy these requirements across perceptual tasks and patient populations.

current_state.text: The Cogitate Consortium study by Ferrante, Gorska-Klimowska, Henin and colleagues was published online on 30 April 2025 and appeared in Nature 642, pages 133–142. It tested preregistered divergent predictions of IIT and GNWT using functional MRI, magnetoencephalography and intracranial EEG across 256 participants. Its findings substantially challenged specified biological predictions of both theories. In particular, the absence of the predicted sustained posterior synchronization challenged the tested IIT implementation, and the general absence of ignition at stimulus offset challenged the tested GNWT prediction.

Other findings supported predictions of the theories. Face–object decoding occurred in posterior and prefrontal regions, and posterior content coding retained support. The experiment focused on biological implementations, leaving the mathematical or computational cores outside its direct tests. Theorists could therefore revise an implementation while retaining a core account. The paper's call for a quantitative framework concerns systematic evidence integration for theory testing and development. The reported findings supply constraints for future accounts without establishing the proposed causal measurement capability.

A diagnostic meta-analysis by Zheng, Tian and Cai, published in Frontiers in Neuroscience on 9 September 2024, examined functional MRI discrimination between unresponsive wakefulness syndrome or vegetative state and minimally conscious state. It included ten studies identified through searches ending in November 2023. The supplied research reports pooled sensitivity and specificity of 0.71 each. The review confirms a summary receiver-operating-characteristic area under the curve of 0.76, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.72–0.80. These estimates describe that diagnostic comparison. Their interpretation is limited by uncertainty in the behavioral reference standard, and they do not establish performance for conscious-content decoding or recovery prediction.

The same meta-analysis cites an approximate residual misdiagnosis rate of 15% when behavioral scales are combined with neuroimaging and electrophysiological techniques. This figure summarizes earlier cited literature, so its applicability depends on the underlying populations and assessment methods. The paper recommends combining neuroimaging with behavioral assessment and other examination techniques. Its discussion of future recovery prediction provides motivation for prospective testing.

General anesthesia already enables reversible changes in responsiveness, consciousness-related behavior and memory. Hu and colleagues' 2024 Neuroscience Bulletin review, volume 40, pages 1995–2011, describes molecular and circuit progress alongside unresolved questions about the networks and specific circuitry involved. Mashour's 2024 Neuron review, volume 112, pages 1553–1567, examines anesthesia as a tool for studying consciousness, including preserved primary sensory processing, disrupted perception and mechanisms of arousal. It emphasizes the distinction between measurable responsiveness and subjective experience. These achievements provide experimental leverage for consciousness research, while leaving selective control and measurement of named conscious contents unestablished by the supplied evidence.

The available evidence is a 2024–2025 snapshot. The supplied freshness record is empty, leaving developments through the intended 1 November 2026 cutoff unverified. Interpretation of the Nature study relies on the passages documented in the supplied review. Its retained article and supplementary extracts are partial, and the largely empty reporting-summary extraction cannot support additional conclusions. The uncaptured Cell abstract cannot substantiate its proposed quotation. The historical systems-neuroscience book extraction contains front matter only, while the tertiary unsolved-problems list documents listed questions with limited authority for establishing the present research frontier.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration one would confirm preregistered predictions in an independent sample, with explicit comparisons against competing theories. Predictions should address the biological findings challenged in 2025 and include conditions in which color, shape and identity are experienced together or dissociated. The theory, analyses, competing predictions and success criteria should be specified before testing. Independent replication should establish how reliably the predictions transfer across the tested tasks and participants.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication confirms preregistered content predictions against competing theories

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration two would use a specified intervention to abolish one reported conscious feature, such as color or face identity, while preserving early sensory responses that the theory predicts can occur without awareness. Controls should assess attention, memory, recognition, reporting and response ability. Reversibility and replication across participants or laboratories would strengthen the causal interpretation. A claim to selectively create or restore content would require a corresponding additional intervention and demonstration.
completion_criteria.label: Abolishing one conscious feature preserves predicted early sensory responses

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration three would prospectively test whether a theory-derived measure improves prediction of later behavioral recovery in disorders of consciousness over a specified multimodal clinical baseline. Outcomes, follow-up intervals, handling of uncertain diagnoses and performance criteria should be prespecified, with validation in an independent clinical cohort. This is a proposed translational benchmark. Recovery prediction provides evidence about prognosis and requires a separate argument to validate particular experienced contents.
completion_criteria.label: Independent clinical validation confirms improved recovery prediction over multimodal baseline

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries would specify which contents, populations, brain states and intervention conditions the account covers, together with uncertainty and failure conditions. Tests should establish measurement reliability and reproducibility within those boundaries. Explaining anesthesia would contribute evidence, while a global change in responsiveness would leave the content-selective criterion unmet. Finite demonstrations establish tested breadth. Extensions to infants, other species, additional sensory modalities or artificial systems would require further validation. These criteria are proposals without established consensus thresholds.
completion_criteria.label: Measurement reliability and reproducibility established within explicit boundaries and uncertainty

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis connects NEU-01, Simultaneous spike-resolved recording from every neuron in one behaving mammalian brain, and NEU-02, Routine synaptic-resolution connectomics of entire mammalian brains, to the measurements and anatomical constraints that could inform a consciousness theory. NEU-03, A prospective theory that predicts mammalian circuit computation from connectivity, shares the demand for prospective mechanistic explanation. Each addresses a distinct target. Comprehensive activity, connectivity or computation predictions would still require an account linking those processes to experienced content.

Roster-based synthesis links NEU-04, Content-faithful reading and writing of specific episodic memories, through the interpretation and manipulation of content. Episodic storage, retrieval and fidelity introduce requirements beyond identifying a current conscious percept. A memory intervention may change later reports through altered recall, making the distinction between memory and ongoing experience important for both concepts.

Roster-based synthesis identifies NEU-07, Noninvasive cellular-resolution read and write through the intact adult human skull, and NEU-09, Cell-type-specific molecular access throughout the intact adult human brain, as potentially enabling measurement and intervention technologies. They address access, targeting and resolution. NEU-10 addresses the interpretation and causal explanation of conscious content, with its own validation requirements.

Roster-based synthesis relates NEU-05, Target-specific regrowth of long axons in the adult mammalian central nervous system, and NEU-06, Reconstruction of human cognitive circuits after neurons have been lost, through possible recovery of pathways and functions supporting experience. NEU-08, A generative developmental code that builds a specified functional neural circuit, concerns constructing circuits with specified functions. These remain distinct regeneration, reconstruction and developmental goals. A causal consciousness account could inform functional assessment if validated for the resulting circuits.

Roster-based synthesis connects NEU-11, Reversible, circuit-specific reopening of critical-period plasticity in the adult brain, through possible controlled changes in perceptual circuitry. NEU-12, A sufficient account of sleep that lets its necessary brain functions be completed without a normal sleep period, overlaps through brain states, arousal and changes in experience. NEU-11 concerns plasticity, NEU-12 concerns fulfilling sleep's necessary functions, and NEU-10 concerns mechanisms and measurements of conscious content.

Feature binding is an internal explanatory target of NEU-10. The explanatory gap remains a question that its operational demonstrations may leave open. Mental causation, including the causal role of reported intention, is a broader related extension. The supplied tertiary list records all of these questions, while providing limited evidence about their present scientific resolution.

The supplied review explicitly confirms the AUC and confidence interval, while the sensitivity and specificity values of 0.71 each are retained from the research notes without separate numerical confirmation in that review.
The approximate 15% residual misdiagnosis estimate depends on earlier cited studies whose populations and methods are not detailed in the supplied review.
Partial Nature article and supplement extractions limit conclusions beyond the reviewed passages. The largely empty reporting-summary extraction adds no usable evidence.
The uncaptured Cell abstract's identity and proposed quotation remain unchecked. The historical book extraction cannot establish the present research frontier.
The proposed demonstrations have no supplied numerical success thresholds, agreed clinical comparator or standardized follow-up interval.
How a measure could be independently validated against experienced content in people unable to report remains an open scientific question.
Whether selective suppression can generalize to selective creation, restoration or broader control of conscious content remains unresolved.
Transfer to infants, other species, additional brain states or artificial implementations remains unestablished.
The proposed operational criteria may leave the explanatory gap and the broader causal role of reported intention unresolved.

brief.title: Explaining and measuring what a person experiences
possible: Seeing a color or recognizing a face could become something scientists can predict, measure and selectively disrupt by changing brain activity. The explanation would also account for how color, shape and identity come together as a single experience.
why: This would connect particular experiences to the brain processes that cause them. It would help explain how activity spread across the brain supports a unified experience.

For patients who cannot reliably respond, better measures of consciousness could improve clinical decisions. A measure that predicts recovery could also help families and clinicians understand a patient's prospects.

sources.showed: This overview lists unresolved questions about experience, including how separate features become a unified perception.
sources.cited_for: It describes the question of how objects, backgrounds and other features combine into an experience.
sources.not_established: Listing these questions does not establish a mechanism or a reliable measure of experience.

sources.showed: The team compared integrated information theory (IIT), based on a network's effects on itself, with global neuronal workspace theory (GNWT), based on information sharing across networks. Results supported some predictions and challenged others.
sources.quote: These results align with some predictions of IIT and GNWT, while substantially challenging key tenets of both theories.
sources.cited_for: Direct comparisons can expose competing explanations of consciousness to tests they might fail.
sources.not_established: The tests challenged proposed brain mechanisms without directly testing either theory's underlying mathematical account.

sources.who: Helin Zheng, Lu Tian and Jinhua Cai
sources.showed: A review found that brain scans helped distinguish patients with minimal signs of awareness from those without behavioral signs. SROC combines diagnostic results across studies; AUC scores their ability to distinguish the groups.
sources.quote: SROC curves showed that the AUC was 0.76
sources.cited_for: Brain scans can contribute to assessing patients whose behavior gives limited clues about consciousness.
sources.not_established: The comparison depends on uncertain behavioral diagnoses and does not establish what patients experience or predict their recovery.

sources.who: Yue Hu, Yun Wang, Lingjing Zhang, Mengqiang Luo and Yingwei Wang
sources.showed: The authors reviewed how anesthesia affects brain networks. Their comparison found that ketamine activated areas that promote wakefulness.
sources.quote: The results demonstrated that ketamine significantly activates cortical and subcortical arousal-promoting nuclei, with the temporal association areas of the cortex as a strong hub.
sources.cited_for: Anesthesia research links changes in consciousness to changes in brain networks.
sources.not_established: Broad changes under anesthesia do not establish selective measurement or control of a particular experienced feature.

sources.showed: Mashour reviewed anesthesia as a tool for studying consciousness. He described findings that distinguish its effects on brain networks from those of sleep.
sources.quote: However, a recent study of intracranial recordings during sleep and anesthesia demonstrated distinct network involvement, with the prefrontal cortex especially affected by anesthesia.
sources.cited_for: Anesthesia offers a way to study changes in consciousness, while responsiveness and experience remain difficult to separate.
sources.not_established: Measuring whether someone responds does not establish whether they have an experience or what it contains.

shown: The Cogitate Consortium tested competing predictions in 256 participants. Brain activity carried information about what people saw, but important predictions from both theories failed. This constrains explanations of consciousness; it does not yet establish which processes cause a particular experience.
missing: A theory still needs independently confirmed predictions of particular experiences and how their features combine.
Selective disruption must change an experienced feature while ruling out problems with attention, memory, recognition or reporting.
Reliable measurements need defined limits, and clinical measures need independent tests of whether they improve recovery prediction.

milestones.label: Independent tests confirm predictions against rival theories
milestones.explanation: Independent researchers would have to confirm predictions fixed before testing, including when features combine or separate, against rival accounts. This would establish predictive reliability.

milestones.label: A feature disappears while early sensory responses remain
milestones.explanation: An intervention would have to abolish a reported feature while preserving predicted early sensory responses and ruling out other impairments. This would connect the feature to a causal brain process.

milestones.label: Clinical tests confirm better recovery predictions
milestones.explanation: An independent patient study would have to show improved recovery prediction over combined clinical assessments, with criteria fixed beforehand. This would establish clinical value for prognosis.

milestones.label: Measurements prove reliable within clearly stated limits
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to establish reliable, reproducible measurements across specified experiences, populations and brain states, with uncertainty stated. This would define where the account works and fails.

uncertain: How can a measure of experienced content be independently validated in someone who cannot report an experience?
It remains unclear whether selectively suppressing a feature could extend to creating or restoring it.
There are no agreed success thresholds for these milestones, and explaining perceptual content may still leave why experience exists unresolved.

page.title: A causal theory of visual consciousness
page.definition: A quantitative theory predicts human visual experiences and how brain interventions change them, with characterized measurement errors. It accounts for feature binding: how colour, shape and other features are experienced as belonging to the same object.

goal.need: Ten studies in a 2024 meta-analysis assessed fMRI discrimination between minimally conscious state and unresponsive wakefulness syndrome. This diagnostic comparison does not identify experienced features. A separate 2025 experiment tested two theories of visual consciousness in 256 participants and challenged predictions of both. These results leave a distinction between classifying clinical states, decoding stimulus information and explaining experienced content.

figures.caption: fMRI diagnostic performance across ten studies in the 2024 meta-analysis.
figures.note: The comparison was minimally conscious state versus unresponsive wakefulness syndrome/vegetative state. These estimates do not validate measurement of particular experienced contents.

statements.quote: The network will develop and provide needed research resources to advance understanding of the neural mechanisms of human consciousness.
statements.context: Research-network concept approved by the advisory council on 17 April 2026.

statements.body: Participants in the NIH/NSF-supported Next Frontiers in Consciousness Research workshop
statements.quote: leverage multiple techniques across spatiotemporal scales, both correlative and causal, to investigate the neural mechanisms of conscious awareness.
statements.context: A recommendation in the workshop report's consensus section.

statements.quote: Convergence on a broadly accepted neuroscientific theory of consciousness will have profound medical, societal and ethical implications.

completion.title: An independently replicated theory predicts visual contents, their binding and intervention effects.
completion.criterion: Within a declared domain of human visual experience, one quantitative theory passes prospectively registered tests of reported features, their binding into objects, and the effects of specified neural interventions. Independent replication meets those tests and establishes measurement errors under the stated conditions. Controls distinguish experiential changes from changes in attention, memory, recognition and reporting. Success applies to the tested contents and conditions.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational criterion; no outside body was found to have published a completion test for this combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of NIH/NSF workshop and programme documents, ASSC materials, NIST/ISO standards and consciousness prizes found no published completion test combining content prediction, binding, intervention and measurement error. This criterion restricts success to reported human visual experience within tested conditions. It combines the published goals of explaining neural mechanisms, using causal methods and testing quantitative predictions. Mashour identifies responsiveness as a confound in measuring experience.

milestones.title: Neural decoding of visible category generalizes across task relevance above 50% chance.
milestones.criterion: A face-versus-object classifier generalizes between task-relevant and task-irrelevant visible stimuli above 50% chance, with a two-sided cluster-based permutation test at P < 0.05. On 30 April 2025, COGITATE reported cross-task decoding in analysed samples of 29 intracranial EEG participants, 65 magnetoencephalography participants and 73 fMRI participants. Decodability establishes represented information, not causal sufficiency.
milestones.set_by: COGITATE Consortium, Experiment 1 multivariate-decoding protocol and the published analysis of visible faces and objects.

milestones.title: Stimulation causes content-specific perceptual distortion absent in sham and nearby-site controls.
milestones.criterion: Neural stimulation produces content-specific perceptual distortion absent during sham stimulation and stimulation of nearby nonselective sites. Parvizi et al., published on 24 October 2012, reported face distortions in one epilepsy patient during seven active trials, absent during four sham trials and three nearby-site trials. Minor nonspecific visual changes were also reported. These observations establish a causal effect on reported perception.
milestones.set_by: Human cortical-stimulation research convention of controlled perturbation, exemplified by Parvizi et al. and Schalk et al.; the quoted comparison concerns face perception.
milestones.threshold_quote: the appearance of faces remained unaffected during both sham stimulation and stimulation of a pair of nearby electrodes that were not face-selective.

milestones.title: Stimulation elicits an additional visual content while the viewed object's appearance is preserved.
milestones.criterion: Stimulation elicits an additional reported visual content while preserving the viewed object's reported appearance, with sham stimulation as a control. Schalk et al., published on 30 October 2017, reported added face percepts and rainbow colours in one 26-year-old epilepsy patient. Colour-preferring sites elicited rainbow or colourful percepts in eight of eight trials; sham stimulation produced no change. This demonstrates elicitation under those conditions.
milestones.set_by: Human cortical-stimulation research convention of content elicitation, demonstrated by Schalk et al.; the published tests concern face and colour percepts.
milestones.threshold_quote: the fact that stimulation of the color-preferring region did not distort the percept of objects but simply added rainbow colors

milestones.title: A theory predicts visual features and their binding in an independent observational test.
milestones.criterion: A fixed quantitative theory predicts reported visual features and their binding into objects in an independent observational dataset, meeting prospectively registered prediction-error criteria. Measurement errors and applicable tasks are characterized. No universal accuracy or reliability cutoff is specified. The cited studies do not establish this combined result; COGITATE's mixed validation outcomes constrain candidate theories.
milestones.set_by: Atlas operational criterion; no published joint content-and-binding validation threshold was found in the NIH/NSF workshop report, NIH programme concept or COGITATE protocol.

not_found: Searches did not locate an outside completion test or agreed numerical accuracy and reliability thresholds for the combined capability.
No published joint validation criterion for quantitative predictions of visual content and feature binding was found.
